title: Writing a will
hook: a Muslim shouldn't spend two nights without a written will (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying for the dead, and the son who asked if charity could still reach his mother. Your line: remember them in du'a. Whose name did you say? Today, something the living can do for the ones they'll leave behind. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

Two nights. That's the window in this hadith, and it's short on purpose. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar reports it, in Sahih al-Bukhari: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase, that it isn't right for a Muslim who has something to leave in a will to spend two nights without that will written down and kept with them. Not two years. Not someday, once things settle down. Two nights. And in the version in Sahih Muslim, Ibn 'Umar adds what he did about it: from the time he heard those words, not a single night passed without his will beside him.
screen: `TWO NIGHTS.` → `WRITTEN, AND KEPT WITH YOU.` → `NOT A NIGHT WITHOUT IT.`

segments.voice: The word is wasiyyah: a will, a bequest, and also a charge, the last instructions you leave in someone's care. The Qur'an speaks of it in surah al-Baqarah, where those near death who leave wealth are told to make a bequest for parents and near relatives, fairly, as a duty on those who are mindful of God. The Qur'an also names fixed shares for heirs, in surah al-Nisa, which is tomorrow's story. The wasiyyah is the part a person shapes for themselves, and a hadith puts a limit on it. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas tells it, also in al-Bukhari. He was ill, and the Prophet came to visit. Sa'd said he had wealth, and only a daughter to inherit, and asked: may I give away all of it in my will? No. Half? No. A third? And the Prophet said, in paraphrase: a third, and a third is a lot. Then he gave the reason: it's better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them poor, holding out their hands to people. So a will in Islam carries two loves at once. Love for the causes and people outside the family, the charity, the friend, the one who has no share. And love for the family, who shouldn't be left in need. Why the hurry, then? The hadith doesn't say. One way to hear it: nobody knows which night is the last. A will written today isn't gloomy. It's kind. It means the people you love won't spend their grief guessing, or arguing, about what you wanted. That's what the wasiyyah protects: their peace, after you.
screen: `WASIYYAH: A WILL, A CHARGE.` · `SA'D ASKS: ALL OF IT?` · `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.` · `NOBODY KNOWS WHICH NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The practice: begin your will. Not the legal document, not today. Just the first page, in your head. Settle and breathe. Think: if this were my last night, what would the people I love need to know? Where things are kept. Who should be looked after. Any debt to repay, any promise to keep. Any cause you'd want a part of what you leave to go to. Let one or two of these become clear. Where you live, the law may have its own requirements, and a real will may need help to write. This is only the beginning of it. The bell holds the time.
Wasiyyah. A will and a final charge, written so the people you leave behind have peace. Today's word.

Your line: write it. Today, write down three things the people you love would need to know, and put the page somewhere they'd find it. Tomorrow, inheritance, lived. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to keep a written will, a wasiyyah, citing the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in al-Bukhari; bequests outside the fixed shares of inheritance are limited to a third of the estate, following the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

fork.setup: you're Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, ill, with wealth and one daughter to inherit. what do you ask the Prophet?
options: can I leave nothing to anyone?
can I give all of it away in my will?
fork.reveal: he asked to give all, then half; the Prophet allowed a third, saying a third is a lot and heirs shouldn't be left in need.

original.note: Arabic: a will, a bequest, a charge left in someone's care.

trapdoor: what you thought: a will is a legal chore for old age.
what it means: in Islam, a written will is something to keep by you now, limited so the family isn't left in need.
what a scholar hears: Ibn 'Umar's 'two nights' in al-Bukhari and Muslim, Sa'd's 'a third, and a third is a lot', and al-Baqarah 2:180 on bequest.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2738 (two nights without a written will)
Sahih Muslim 1627 (Ibn 'Umar: not a night passed without my will)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2742 (Sa'd: a third, and a third is a lot)
Qur'an 2:180 (bequest for parents and near relatives)

notes: Editor: the reason for the 'two nights' urgency is now framed as a reading, since the hadith gives no reason.
Bukhari 2738, 2742 and Muslim 1627 paraphrased; confirm numbers and details (Sa'd's only daughter; the visit in illness).

Qur'an 2:180 paraphrased; jurists generally hold that the bequest to heirs in 2:180 was later governed by the inheritance verses. The script avoids the abrogation question; Keeper to check the framing of the will beside the fixed shares of surah al-Nisa.
Practice notes that local law may have its own requirements; this is not legal advice.
